children: HEADLINES
Retail Sales Recover Following First Fall of Year in July
Canadian retail sales are tracking for a rebound in August after a broad retreat in spending the month before led to the first pullback in retail trade this year.
An advance estimate by Statistics Canada indicates sales rose 1.3% last month, which given goods prices were largely unchanged hints at an increase in trade volumes as well.

It comes after sales in July declined 0.7% from the previous month to a seasonally adjusted 73.7 billion Canadian dollars, the equivalent of about US$52.25 billion, data released Thursday showed. That was the first retreat for retailers since December. In volume terms, sales were down an even sharper 1.1% for the month, indicating Canadians bought less overall.
BlackBerry Lifts Outlook on Automotive Software Revenue Demand
BlackBerry is expanding its automotive software footprint, defying broader sector headwinds, capitalizing on surging demand for high-performance computing into new models.
Shares in Toronto rose 3.6% to C$12.27.

The momentum delivered a second-quarter earnings beat, prompting the company to raise its full-year forecast. Growth largely came from its QNX embedded software unit, which posted a 27% revenue surge, driving total revenue up 26% to $163.3 million, handily beating Wall Street forecasts.

"The market itself could be a little bit choppy because of the geopolitical and the macro type of things, but we are really well positioned," Chief Executive John Giamatteo said in an interview. "It's just a natural progression of technology: more software, more sophistication, more software domains are going into the car."
Carney Open to U.S. Trade Deal But Won't Give Up Right to Deepen EU Ties

A mutually beneficial trade pact between Canada and the U.S. is still possible, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, but his country won't give up its freedom to strike deals with the European Union and other parts of the world as it seeks to diversify global connections and protect its national sovereignty.

Trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed in August, with President Trump imposing steep tariffs and Canada retaliating with levies of its own. In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Carney indicated that some progress had been achieved since then, but not enough to clinch a deal.

"There were a series of issues late in the negotiations that were red lines for us, that we couldn't cross and didn't cross. Some of those have been taken off the table," Carney said. "But one of the core principles here...is we're not going to compromise our sovereignty. Our ability to pursue trade deals with other jurisdictions is very important to us."
Jeep Maker Stellantis, Stingray Agree to Embed TuneIn App in Future Vehicles
Canadian streaming media company Stingray agreed with automaker Stellantis to integrate its streaming application natively into future vehicles.
Stingray will provide its TuneIn service, bringing a large catalog of over 100,000 radio stations--from breaking news to curated music--to Stellantis' lineup of upcoming models.
No financial details for the agreement were provided.
Payroll Employment Continues to Rise
Payroll numbers in Canada ticked up in July, building on gains in recent months even as job vacancies in the country remain little changed.

The number of employees receiving pay and benefits from an employer rose by 26,100, or 0.1%, for the month. That followed gains totaling 124,200 from March to June. On a year earlier, payroll employment was up 171,900 in July. For a seventh straight month, there was little movement in vacancies, which sat at 501,000 jobs.

The data offers a counterpoint to Statistics Canada's more timely labor force survey. That survey pointed to a 41,700 drop in Canadian employment in August, pulling back on July's strong 75,100 gain but leaving the jobless rate steady at 6.4%.
Business Optimism in Canada Slumps With Fuel-Price Worries
Optimism among small businesses in Canada has fallen sharply over both the near and longer term, the latest business barometer by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business showed.
The outlook on a three-month and a 12-month basis now sits below the 50 neutral mark, retreating 9.6 points to 43.3 and 9.8 point to 47.9, respectively.

Director of economics Andreea Bourgeois noted businesses are pointing to fuel costs as the top constraint on growth. As well, the survey found that companies trading only in Canadian markets are more optimistic than those trading outside the country, exporting or importing.
TALKING POINT
The Group Chat Where World Leaders Are Racing to Create AI Controls
By Maxwell Zeff, Drew Hinshaw and Joe Parkinson

Norway's prime minister thumbed out a text message to an increasingly familiar contact on his phone-a fellow head of government he hoped would join a nascent plan of Western leaders to design a new framework to regulate artificial intelligence.
Jonas Gahr Støre said that within 10 minutes, Canada's Mark Carney had texted back: "Of course. We're in."

Around the same time, Carney was discussing AI regulation with French President Emmanuel Macron on a French island in the Atlantic 12 miles off the Canadian coast, as Macron's government called on the United Nations Security Council to focus on AI and security ahead of Wednesday's General Assembly. By Monday, Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb had published a two-page paper arguing that AI "must remain under human direction, oversight and control" and suggested creating a global supervisory regime.
A club of Western presidents and prime ministers is leading a new push for global controls on AI, echoing the nuclear arms treaties that took root during the first decades of the Atomic Era.

In conversations with The Wall Street Journal, leaders and their aides described a global system in which the world's top AI innovator-the U.S.-is, in their view, reluctant to address the potential risks of a technology powering America's stock gains and economic growth.
Carney has proposed a global "technology stability" body that would help set norms and constraints.

"There are leaders that step forward and say, 'OK, where can we take responsibility, come together?'" said Støre, speaking from Ottawa, where he had spent the day in meetings with Carney. "I hear the American president saying, you know, 'The only thing that matters is beating China in the competition.'"
In his address to the U.N. on Tuesday, President Trump said the U.S. would reject any "globalist scheme" to control AI.
The White House director of science and technology policy spoke at the U.N. on Wednesday and warned that international dialogue "cannot be allowed to drift towards global governance."
"The frontier of intelligence is advancing rapidly," Michael Kratsios said. "That is not a reason to pause its further development, or to constrain it with new global governance structures."

Many analysts say any global standards body that doesn't have the buy-in of the U.S. and Chinese governments would likely have a limited impact. So far, the countries pushing hardest for global guardrails are consumers rather than innovators and incubators of the world's top AI companies, but several of America's leading AI developers are also calling for global AI rules.

"If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people they serve," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in his Wednesday address to the U.N. "In our history, there have been times where countries who compete and don't always like each other very much still come together for shared interests and collective good in the face of a powerful new technology. We believe this must be one of those times."

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei offered suggestions the U.N. Security Council could implement to cooperate on AI safety, such as an international ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and the creation of evaluation systems to track global AI progress.

"I believe that this is the most important global security issue facing the world today," he said. "For all the differences of the people in this room, we must put aside those differences in order to confront this global opportunity and global threat that is being presented to us at the same time. No leader, no company and no nation can manage this alone."
Altman and Amodei used their U.N. speeches to call for the creation of a global body to set AI standards, which both companies have advocated for in recent months.

The comments echo a July proposal from Demis Hassabis, the chair of Google DeepMind and previously its CEO, suggesting the U.S. government and tech industry should collaborate to create an AI standards body modeled after the Financial Industry Regulation Authority, or Finra.

Hassabis said AI developers could voluntarily submit models for evaluation up to 30 days before release, and that the U.S.-initiated effort would be a "strong starting point for creating shared international standards on frontier AI."

The idea gained traction with some companies and some Trump administration officials, but stalled after Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Elon Musk of SpaceX told the president they opposed the concept.

Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue also addressed the U.N. on Wednesday and called for greater transparency into private companies developing cutting-edge AI models. He pushed for the broad dissemination of open-source AI models, which can be downloaded freely and used at a low cost.
While Hugging Face was the victim of a widely-publicized AI-powered hack from models OpenAI was testing internally, Delangue said the AI industry shouldn't stoke fear among the public.

"We strongly believe that fear-based narratives are not the way to make the right decisions about the future of such a foundational and empowering technology or bring the public along with us," said Delangue.
